title: Chapter 51: Supreme Courage 1
content:
Chapter 51

Yunmeng was a land carved by water, and the ancestral home of its leading cultivation sect—the Yunmeng Jiang Clan’s Lotus Pier—sat built directly upon the lakes.

Cast off from the docks of Lotus Pier and row downstream for just a little while, and you'd find yourself drifting into an endless expanse of lotus ponds spanning hundreds of miles, known as Lotus Lake. Broad emerald leaves nudged against each other shoulder to shoulder, crowding beneath slender pink blooms standing proud in the breeze. Whenever the wind swept across the water, the blossoms and leaves would sway and bob in unison, looking for all the world like an army of polite, nodding heads—a sight as delightfully goofy as it was gorgeous.

Unlike the secluded, untouchable sanctuaries of other great clans—places hidden away behind locked gates where ordinary mortals were forbidden from stepping foot within miles—Lotus Pier had never set itself apart from the everyday world. The wide stone docks right outside its front gates were always bustling, packed with vendors squatting over baskets of fresh lotus seeds, water caltrops, and piping hot street snacks. Even the neighborhood kids could wipe their runny noses on their sleeves and sneak into the training grounds to gawk at sword drills; nobody ever yelled at them for trespassing, and every now and then, the young Jiang disciples would even invite them to join their games.

Back in his youth, Wei Wuxian loved nothing more than shooting kites down by the shores of Lotus Lake.

Jiang Cheng kept his eyes glued to his own kite, glancing sideways every few seconds to measure up Wei Wuxian’s. Wei Wuxian’s kite was already soaring high in the clouds, yet he hadn't made a single move to notch an arrow. Instead, he stood with his right hand shading his eyes, face turned up to the sky with a grin, apparently deciding it still hadn't drifted far enough.

Seeing the target on the verge of slipping past his guaranteed range, Jiang Cheng gritted his teeth, drew his bowstring taut, and let fly. A white-fletched arrow whistled into the sky, punching clean through the eye of the one-eyed monster painted on his kite, sending it tumbling down. Jiang Cheng’s scowl smoothed out, and he smirked, “Bullseye!”

A beat later, he threw a challenge: “Yours is out in the middle of nowhere. Think you can still hit it?”

Wei Wuxian just grinned. “Take a guess.”

Only then did he casually pluck an arrow from his quiver and take aim. He drew the bow until it formed a full moon, then loosed the string with a sharp snap.

Dead center!

Jiang Cheng’s scowl returned in full force, and he let out an irritated snort. The surrounding boys stowed their bows and bolted down the banks, scrambling to retrieve the kites and rank the scores. Whoever had the shortest shot was dead last, and without fail, that dishonor always fell on the Sixth Shidi. The poor kid was routinely roasted by the whole squad, but he had skin thick enough to bounce arrows off of and couldn't care less. Wei Wuxian’s shot was easily the farthest, with Jiang Cheng’s sitting in a close second; naturally, neither of them could be bothered to go fetch their own. A pack of boys tore into the covered Nine-Bend Lotus Corridor, leaping across the boardwalks and chasing each other over the railings, when two slender figures suddenly stepped into their path.

Both were young women dressed in the crisp garb of armed handmaidens, short swords slung at their waists. The taller of the two blocked the walkway, holding up a punctured kite and an arrow, her voice dropping cold: “Whose is this?”

The moment the boys saw who it was, their hearts collectively sank. Wei Wuxian rubbed his chin, stepping forward with an easy shrug. “Mine.”

The other maid scoffed, “Well, at least you’re honest.”

The two maids parted to either side, making way for a sword-bearing woman draped in regal purple robes.

She was striking, with porcelain-fair skin and finely chiseled features, though her sharp gaze carried an icy, razor-thin edge. The faint, mocking curve of her lips was an effortless sneer—a signature look she’d passed straight down to Jiang Cheng. Her frame was lithe and graceful beneath the rich purple silk, her pale face and the hand resting on her sword hilt cold as carved jade. Circling her right index finger was an ornate ring set with a deep amethyst.

Jiang Cheng’s face lit up with an eager smile. “A-Niang!”

The rest of the boys bowed low, dropping their rowdy swagger in an instant. “Madam Yu.”

Madam Yu was Jiang Cheng’s mother, Yu Ziyuan. She was Jiang Fengmian’s wife and had once been his fellow cultivation peer. By all rights, society should have addressed her as Madam Jiang, but for reasons nobody questioned, everyone had always called her Madam Yu. Word had it that her unyielding pride made her loathe taking her husband's family name; either way, neither husband nor wife had ever bothered to correct it.

Hailing from the prominent Meishan Yu Clan, she was the third child of her generation, earning her the title of San-niangzi. In the cultivation world, she went by the moniker of the Violet Spider—a name that was more than enough to make grown men flinch. Since youth, she had been notoriously sharp-tongued and cold-blooded, fiercely antisocial and utterly unapologetic about it. Even after marrying Jiang Fengmian, she spent most of the year out on rogue night-hunts, rarely bothering to linger in Lotus Pier. Her living quarters here were completely separated from Jiang Fengmian’s, occupying a private pavilion inhabited solely by her and the personal retinue she’d brought from the Yu family. These two young maidens, Jinzhu and Yinzhu, were her most trusted confidantes and never left her side.

Madam Yu swept her gaze over Jiang Cheng, her tone dry. “Fooling around again? Come here and let me look at you.”

Jiang Cheng shuffled over. She gave his arm a sharp pinch with her slender fingers, followed by a harsh smack to his shoulder. “Not an ounce of progress in your cultivation! You’re pushing seventeen, yet you still run around like a brainless toddler making trouble every single day. Do you think you’re like the rest of them? Who knows what gutter they’ll end up crawling through, but you—you are the future head of the Jiang Clan!”

Jiang Cheng swayed slightly under the hit, keeping his chin tucked, not daring to talk back. Wei Wuxian didn't need a translator to know that little barb was aimed directly at his forehead. One of the junior disciples caught his eye and stuck his tongue out in silent sympathy; Wei Wuxian just shot him an amused wink.

Madam Yu’s eyes snapped toward him. “Wei Ying, what ridiculous face are you pulling now?”

Accustomed to the routine, Wei Wuxian stepped out of the group. Madam Yu sneered, “Always that same look! If you have no ambition to make something of yourself, fine, but stop dragging Jiang Cheng into the dirt with you. You're ruining him.”

Wei Wuxian put on a face of pure, theatrical shock. “Me, lacking ambition? Madam Yu, isn't it an open secret that I'm the hardest worker in Lotus Pier?”

Teenagers weren't known for their restraint, and he just couldn't resist a snappy retort. The second the words left his mouth, Madam Yu’s brow twitched with murderous intent.

Jiang Cheng cut in desperately, “Wei Wuxian, shut up!”

He turned to his mother, trying to defuse the bomb: “It’s not like we actively wanted to stay cooped up shooting kites in the yard, but nobody can leave right now anyway! The Wen Clan has claimed every decent hunting ground in the region as their private territory. Even if I wanted to go on a night-hunt, there’s nowhere left to go. Didn’t you and Father specifically tell us to stay home, keep our heads down, and not get into scraps with the Wen Clan over prey?”

Madam Yu let out a chilling laugh. “Oh, don't worry. This time, even if you want to stay home, you won't have a choice.”

Jiang Cheng blinked, caught off guard. Ignoring the boys, Madam Yu raised her chin and swept past them down the corridor, her two handmaidens throwing venomous daggers at Wei Wuxian before falling in step behind their mistress.

Come dinner, the meaning behind her words became dreadfully clear.

A royal envoy had arrived from the Qishan Wen Clan with an imperial-style mandate: under the flimsy pretext that the other clans were 'inept at proper instruction and letting young talents go to waste,' every sect was ordered to dispatch at least twenty disciples to Qishan within three days, where Wen masters would personally 're-educate' them.

Jiang Cheng was flabbergasted. “Are they serious? The sheer, shameless audacity!”

Wei Wuxian snorted, “Well, when you think of yourself as the sun hanging over the entire cultivation world, why wouldn't you? It's not like the Wen Clan being shameless is breaking news. Throwing their weight around since last year, banning everyone else from night-hunting, snatching up everyone’s prey, and seizing whole territories...”

Seated at the head of the hall, Jiang Fengmian set down his cup. “Watch your tongue. Eat your dinner.”

The grand banquet hall was cavernous, currently housing only the five of them, each seated behind a low square table bearing simple dishes. Wei Wuxian picked up his chopsticks, only to feel a gentle tug at his sleeve. Looking up, he saw Jiang Yanli offering him a small ceramic dish filled with freshly peeled lotus seeds—plump, milky white, and bursting with sweet juice.

Wei Wuxian leaned in, whispering, “Thanks, Shijie.”

Jiang Yanli offered a warm, gentle smile, her soft features instantly coming alive with quiet grace.

Across the room, Madam Yu’s voice sliced through the warmth like ice: “What's the point of eating? Once they arrive in Qishan in a few days, who knows if they'll even be given scraps? They might as well skip a few meals right now and get their stomachs used to starving!”

The Wen Clan’s demand was an offer no one could refuse. History was littered with bloody precedents: any sect reckless enough to defy their decrees was instantly branded with wild accusations like 'instigating sect rebellion' or 'endangering the cultivation world,' providing the Wen Clan with a righteous, high-and-mighty excuse to wipe them off the map.

Jiang Fengmian replied in his usual unhurried, even tone, “Why work yourself into such a state? Whatever tomorrow brings, we still have to eat today.”

Madam Yu’s patience snapped. She slammed her palm onto the table. “Work myself into a state?! Ishouldbe in a state! How can you sit there acting so calm and indifferent? Did you not hear the demands that messenger spat out? A mere servant girl had the gall to swagger into my home and order me around! And those twenty disciples—they specifically demanded direct heirs from the main bloodline! What does that mean? It means between A-Cheng and A-Li, at least one of them has to go! 'Re-education'? Since when does the Wen Clan get a say in how other families raise their children?! This isn't schooling—they’re demanding hostages to wrap around their fingers!”

Jiang Cheng spoke up quickly, “A-Niang, please don't be angry. I'll go. It's fine.”

Madam Yu rounded on him. “Of course you're going! Did you think we’d send your sister? Look at her, sitting there happily peeling lotus seeds like an idiot. A-Li, drop those! Who are you peeling those for? You are the young mistress of this house, not someone else's servant!”

Hearing the word 'servant,' Wei Wuxian didn't bat an eye. He tipped the entire dish into his mouth, chewing down the sweet, refreshing crunch with total nonchalance.

Jiang Fengmian, however, looked up from his bowl. “San-niang.”

Madam Yu flared, “Did I say something wrong? 'Servant'? What, does hearing that word upset your delicate sensibilities? Tell me, Jiang Fengmian, do you plan on sendinghimthis time?”

Jiang Fengmian said mildly, “It's his choice. If he wishes to go, he goes.”

Wei Wuxian raised a hand immediately. “I'm going.”

Madam Yu let out a venomous laugh. “How convenient! Going if he wants, staying if he doesn't. Why does A-Cheng have no choice in the matter? Truly, Sect Leader Jiang, you're quite the saint when it comes to raising other people’s sons!”

Resentment had been festering in her chest for years, and now she was simply venting her bitter rage without a shred of logic. The rest of the table stayed dead silent, letting the storm pass.

Jiang Fengmian murmured, “San-niangzi, you are tired. Go back and rest.”

Jiang Cheng looked up at her from his seat. “A-Niang...”

Madam Yu rose to her feet, looking down at her son with pure derision. “What are you calling me for? Telling me to hold my tongue, just like your father? You foolish boy, I told you long ago: you won't ever measure up to the one sitting next to you! You can't beat him in cultivation, you can't beat him on a night-hunt, you can't even beat him at shooting a kite! But what choice do you have? Whose fault is it that your mother can't compare to his? You just can't measure up, plain and simple! I fight tooth and nail for your sake, warned you a hundred times not to fool around with him, and you still have the nerve to defend him! How did I ever give birth to a son like you?!”

She stormed out of the hall, leaving Jiang Cheng sitting frozen, his face cycling from pale to flushed with humiliated fury. Without a word, Jiang Yanli quietly slid another small dish of freshly peeled lotus seeds onto his table.

After a lingering hush, Jiang Fengmian broke the silence: “I will select eighteen more disciples tonight. You depart at dawn.”

Jiang Cheng nodded stiffly, his tongue tied. He had never figured out how to talk to his father, whereas Wei Wuxian navigated it with effortless ease.

Draining his soup bowl, Wei Wuxian grinned, “Uncle Jiang, don't you have any parting gifts for us?”

Jiang Fengmian offered a faint, warm smile. “I gave you what you needed long ago: your swords at your hips, and our clan motto in your hearts.”

Wei Wuxian perked up. “Ah!'Attempt the impossible,'right?”

Jiang Cheng snapped an immediate glare his way. “That doesn't mean go looking for impossible trouble on purpose!”

The heavy gloom over the table finally broke, dissolving into a much-needed breath of life.

The next morning, having run through the necessary logistics, Jiang Fengmian left them with a single parting thought: “The disciples of Yunmeng Jiang are made of sturdier stuff than to break at the first gust of wind from the outside world.”

Jiang Yanli walked with them step for step, accompanying them down the road as far as she could, stuffing every pocket and pack she could reach full of rations and dried snacks, terrified they’d starve in Qishan. Laden down with a small mountain of food, the twenty boys set out from Lotus Pier, arriving at the designated 'Re-education Office' in Qishan just before the deadline.

Young cultivators from clans across the realm were already gathered in the square, scattered in tense clumps. Among the hundreds present, many recognized one another from past conferences. Whispering in hushed groups of three or four, their grim faces made it glaringly obvious that none of them had arrived here on pleasant terms.

Scanning the sea of robes, Wei Wuxian murmured, “Looks like Gusu had to send a contingent too.”

For reasons unknown, the disciples representing the Gusu Lan Clan looked unusually exhausted. Lan Wangji’s complexion was particularly pale, though his expression remained as icy and distant as ever. With his sword Bichen strapped across his back, he stood completely alone, an island of frost in the middle of the crowd.

Wei Wuxian took a step forward to greet him, but Jiang Cheng caught his arm with a sharp hiss: “Don't start trouble!” He reluctantly backed off.

Suddenly, a loud voice barked commands from up ahead, ordering the assembled heirs to fall into formation before a raised terrace. A squad of Wen disciples pushed through the ranks, shouting, “Quiet down! No talking!”

The young man standing on the platform looked barely nineteen, strutting with immense arrogance. His face could generously be called handsome, but much like his slick hair, he gave off a greasy, suffocating vibe. It was none other than the youngest son of the Qishan Wen Sect Leader, Wen Chao.

Wen Chao was notoriously fond of the spotlight, rarely missing a chance to show off before the other clans, making his face all too familiar to the crowd. Flanking him like bodyguards were two figures. On his left stood a stunning girl with a supple figure, willow-leaf brows, and scarlet lips; the only flaw was a dark mole sitting just above her lip—a blemish so poorly placed you practically itched to scrape it off. On his right stood a broad-shouldered man in his late twenties, looking impassive, radiating an imposing, heavy aura.

Looking down at the sea of heirs from his high vantage point, Wen Chao puffed out his chest, thoroughly drunk on his own importance. He waved a flippant hand. “Line up and surrender your swords, one by one!”

The crowd erupted into an angry buzz. Someone shouted, “A cultivator’s sword never leaves their side! Why should we hand them over?!”

Wen Chao’s voice snapped across the platform: “Who said that? Which clan are you from? Step out!”

The speaker choked on his words, shrinking back into the ranks. Seeing the crowd fall obediently quiet, Wen Chao smiled with smug satisfaction. “It's precisely because disciples like you lack basic manners, obedience, and respect for authority that I decided you needed to be disciplined in the first place. You’re this reckless now; if I don't knock you into shape early on, who knows when you'll get it into your heads to challenge your betters and climb all over the Wen Clan's heads!”

Everyone knew his demand for their weapons was purely malicious, but with the Wen Clan currently reigning supreme, every other sect was walking on broken glass. Terrified that the slightest resistance would result in their entire family being wiped out on trumped-up charges, they had no choice but to swallow the insult and comply.

Jiang Cheng held a firm grip on Wei Wuxian’s arm. Wei Wuxian whispered out of the side of his mouth, “What are you grabbing me for?”

Jiang Cheng muttered, “Making sure you don't do anything stupid.”

“Give me some credit,” Wei Wuxian scoffed softly. “The guy's a greasy piece of work, but even if I wanted to break his nose, I wouldn't pick right now and drag our clan into a war. Relax.”

Jiang Cheng eyed him warily. “Planning to throw a sack over his head in an alley again? Hate to break it to you, but that won't fly here. See that guy standing next to him?”

“I see him,” Wei Wuxian murmured. “High cultivation, but looks a bit aged. Late bloomer, probably.”

“That’s Wen Zhuliu,” Jiang Cheng warned, his voice dropping lower. “They call him the 'Core-Melting Hand.' He's Wen Chao's personal escort, tasked specifically with guarding him. Don't touch him.”

Wei Wuxian’s brow twitched. “'Core-Melting Hand'?”

“Yeah. Those palms of his are lethal, and he's completely loyal to the tyrant. Before this, he helped Wen...”

Staring straight ahead, the two boys cut their whispers the second a Wen attendant approached to collect their blades. Wei Wuxian casually unclipped his sword and handed it over, his eyes drifting reflexively toward the Gusu Lan contingent. He’d fully expected Lan Wangji to refuse, but to his surprise, despite looking frosty enough to freeze the air solid, Lan Wangji unbuckled his sword without a word.

Madam Yu’s bitter parting shot had turned out to be an accurate prophecy: their daily rations in Qishan were nothing more than watery gruel. The delicious dry provisions Jiang Yanli had packed for them had been confiscated on day one, and with none of these young disciples anywhere near reaching inedia, their stomachs spent every waking hour growling in misery.

As for the Wen Clan’s grand 're-education,' it amounted to handing out copies of theWen Clan Anthology of Virtues—a dense, tedious scripture detailing the glorious exploits and lofty quotes of past Wen clan leaders, demanding that everyone memorize it by heart. Every morning, Wen Chao would mount his high platform to drone on, demanding thunderous cheers and commanding them to treat his every breath as a divine role model.

Whenever they went out on 'night-hunts,' he forced the guest heirs to march ahead as human bait—scouting dark trails, drawing the attention of fierce beasts, and brawling through bloody skirmishes. Once the monster was battered within an inch of its life, Wen Chao would swoop in for the kill, lop off its head, and spend the rest of the day bragging about his peerless solo victory. If someone caught his eye in the wrong way, he’d drag them up and chew them out publicly, berating them like dogs.

Two years ago, during the archery contest at the Qishan grand conference, Wen Chao had entered the field alongside Wei Wuxian and the rest. Fully convinced he’d take the championship, he’d taken it for granted that the other heirs would yield to him. Instead, his first three shots were an absolute trainwreck: one hit, one miss, and one pierced the wrong target. Protocol dictated an immediate elimination, but he refused to step down, and the other clans had been too polite to call him out. When the scores were tallied, the top four spots belonged to Wei Wuxian, Lan Xichen, Jin Zixuan, and Lan Wangji. Had Lan Wangji not walked off the range early, his score would have been even higher.

Humiliated beyond measure, Wen Chao nursed a burning grudge against those four in particular. With Lan Xichen absent, he spent his days dragging the other three onto the platform to publicly berate them, thoroughly enjoying his petty power trip.

Jin Zixuan had it the worst. Raised as the pampered darling of his clan, he’d never swallowed an insult in his life; if not for his fellow Jin disciples desperately holding him back and the terrifying presence of Wen Zhuliu, he would have drawn steel and gone down fighting on day one. Lan Wangji, on the other hand, existed in a state of absolute, detached serenity—looking through everything with vacant eyes, as though his soul had long since left his body.

As for Wei Wuxian? Having survived years of Madam Yu’s colorful, creative daily tongue-lashings back at Lotus Pier, stepping off the platform with a grin was second nature. Wen Chao’s pathetic attempts at insults weren't even on the same playing field.

Today, the disciples were dragged awake at the crack of dawn once again, herded through the trails like livestock toward a new night-hunt destination.

Their target: Mount Muxi.

The deeper they pressed into the mountains, the thicker the canopy grew overhead, casting long, suffocating shadows across the forest floor. Aside from the rustling sea of leaves and the plodding rhythm of footsteps, the wilderness was dead quiet; the sudden shriek of a bird or bug felt unnervingly loud in the gloom.

After hours of marching, the trail converged with a bubbling mountain brook. Red maple leaves drifted along the clear water, their crisp color and the gentle rush of the current washing away a fraction of the oppressive gloom, accompanied by the faint, lilting giggles of girls up ahead.

Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng trudged along, muttering creative curses against the Wen dogs under their breath, when Wei Wuxian happened to glance over his shoulder.

A flash of white robes caught his eye: Lan Wangji was walking just a short distance behind them.

Slowing his pace, Lan Wangji had drifted toward the rear of the column. Over the past few days, Wei Wuxian had tried breaking the ice and catching up several times, but every single time, Lan Wangji would turn on his heel and walk the other way, while Jiang Cheng constantly warned him not to poke the bear.

Now that they were closer, Wei Wuxian couldn't help but study him more carefully. Though Lan Wangji was clearly trying his best to walk normally, Wei Wuxian noticed that his right foot hit the ground significantly lighter than his left, careful not to bear any real weight.

Seeing this, Wei Wuxian dropped his pace, falling in step beside him.

"What happened to your leg?"
